Makkedah
mak-KEE-dah
proper noun
Hebrew Maqqedah, perhaps “place of shepherds” or “herding place,” a town of the Judahite lowland.

📖 Biblical Definition

Makkedah was a town in the lowland of Judah, made memorable by the cave wherein the five Amorite kings hid themselves in the day of the LORD’s great victory at Gibeon. When the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon fled before Israel, they hid in the cave at Makkedah; and it was told Joshua, who commanded great stones to be rolled upon the mouth of the cave and men set to keep it, while Israel pursued and smote their enemies (Jos 10:16–21). Then Joshua bade them open the cave and bring out the five kings, and he laid his foot upon their necks before the captains of his men of war, saying, “Fear not, nor be dismayed, be strong and of good courage: for thus shall the LORD do to all your enemies” (Jos 10:25). He smote them and slew them, and hanged them on five trees until the evening, and at sundown cast their bodies into the cave and laid great stones upon its mouth. That same day Joshua took Makkedah, and smote it with the edge of the sword, doing to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho (Jos 10:28). The town is numbered afterward among the cities of Judah in the lowland (Jos 15:41). Makkedah stands as one of the great monuments of the conquest, where the LORD made plain that He fights for His people and treads down their proud enemies; and the foot of Joshua upon the necks of the kings is a figure of the victory of the greater Joshua over every power of darkness.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town of the Judahite lowland whose cave hid the five Amorite kings, whom Joshua slew and hanged.

expand to see more

MAKKEDAH, a town in the lowland of Judah (Jos 15:41).

The five Amorite kings hid in its cave after the rout at Gibeon (Jos 10:16).

Joshua shut the cave with great stones and kept it (Jos 10:18).

He brought out the kings, set his foot on their necks, and slew them (Jos 10:24–26).

He took the city and smote it with the edge of the sword (Jos 10:28).

📖 Key Scripture

Jos 10:16 — "But these five kings fled, and hid themselves in a cave at Makkedah."

Jos 10:24 — "And it came to pass, when they brought out those kings unto Joshua, that Joshua called for all the men of Israel, and said unto the captains of the men of war which went with him, Come near, put your feet upon the necks of these kings. And they came near, and put their feet upon the necks of them."

Jos 10:28 — "And that day Joshua took Makkedah, and smote it with the edge of the sword, and the king thereof he utterly destroyed, them, and all the souls that were therein; he let none remain: and he did to the king of Makkedah as he did unto the king of Jericho."

Jos 15:41 — "And Gederoth, Bethdagon, and Naamah, and Makkedah; sixteen cities with their villages:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD’s faithfulness in treading down the enemies of His people.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s faithfulness in giving the land and casting down its proud kings. At Makkedah the five Amorite kings who had warred against Gibeon were drawn from their hiding cave and slain, and Joshua charged Israel, “thus shall the LORD do to all your enemies.” What God had sworn to the fathers He performed, subduing the strongholds of Canaan one by one; the conquest was no work of mere men but the LORD’s own war for His covenant people.

The foot of Joshua upon the necks of the kings typifies the believer’s inheritance and victory in Christ, the greater Joshua. As the captains of Israel set their feet upon the necks of their fallen enemies, so the Lord Jesus has bruised Satan under the feet of His people and will shortly tread him down altogether (Rom 16:20). The cave at Makkedah, sealed with great stones over the bodies of the kings, stands a lasting monument that every power arrayed against the people of God shall be brought low and shut up under His judgment.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name perhaps means “place of shepherds,” borne by the town of the cave of the five kings.

expand to see more

Makkedah — Hebrew Maqqedah, perhaps “place of shepherds.”

It lay in the lowland of Judah.

Its cave hid the five Amorite kings.

Joshua slew the kings and hanged them on five trees.

He took the city and utterly destroyed it.

Usage

"Like Makkedah, the LORD treads down the proud enemies of His people and keeps every word of His covenant."

"Joshua’s foot upon the kings’ necks teaches that God subdues all foes before His people."

"The greater Joshua bruises Satan under His saints’ feet, as the kings were trodden down at Makkedah."
